analysis.one_liner: Replaces Clean Water Act permits for ship discharges with uniform Coast Guard standards and overrides stricter state rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013, without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Ships routinely discharge ballast water and other wastewater into U.S. waters, which can spread invasive species. This bill would move regulation of those discharges from the Environmental Protection Agency's Clean Water Act permitting system to a single set of national standards written by the Coast Guard, and it would generally stop states from enforcing their own, potentially stricter, discharge rules [S2] [S3]. It sets numeric treatment targets for ballast water starting around 2020, requires certification of treatment technology, and grandfathers equipment already installed on ships for the rest of its service life [S3]. Introduced in June 2012 with bipartisan support, it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received any further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial shipping operators gain most: one national standard replaces a patchwork of EPA permits and state rules, already-installed treatment systems are grandfathered until the end of their service life, and fishing, recreational, and small commercial vessels are exempted outright. Ballast water treatment manufacturers gain a guaranteed market, since certified systems become the only legal way to comply [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Establishes uniform national discharge standards that supersede any other permitting requirement or discharge prohibition for vessel operations, replacing the Clean Water Act permit regime for these discharges [S3].

Bars states from adopting or enforcing their own vessel discharge rules, except for stricter ballast water standards that already existed and survive a petition process with a 90-day filing window after enactment [S3].

Exempts commercial vessels under 79 feet, fishing vessels, and recreational vessels from any permit or discharge standard, and grandfathers installed ballast treatment systems for the rest of their service life even if standards tighten later [S3].
Makes this Act the exclusive federal statutory authority for regulating these discharges, which removes parallel Clean Water Act permitting and enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the waters and the people who depend on them in states that had adopted or wanted stricter ballast water rules, since those rules are generally preempted and the new national standard is subject to a feasibility review that can weaken or delay it. Removing Clean Water Act permitting also eliminates a separate avenue of public enforcement, leaving Coast Guard standards as the only check [S3].

drawbacks.text: Section 10 generally prohibits states from adopting or enforcing their own vessel discharge rules after enactment, with only a narrow savings clause for pre-existing stricter ballast standards that a governor must petition to keep within 90 days [S3].

The 2020 revised ballast water performance standard takes effect only after a feasibility review weighing costs and impacts on shipping, and if no certified technology can meet it the Secretary may fall back to 'the best treatment technology available' and extend deadlines by up to 24 months per vessel class [S3].
Grandfathering lets a vessel run a treatment system installed under older, weaker standards until the end of that system's service life, even after standards are revised upward [S3].

Because the Act is the exclusive federal authority for these discharges, the Clean Water Act's permitting and enforcement tools no longer apply, concentrating all regulatory power in the Coast Guard's standards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a genuine upside: it would finally impose numeric ballast water treatment targets and a technology certification system aimed at keeping invasive species out of U.S. waters, and uniform national rules do give ship operators predictability. But the design tilts toward the industry asking for it. The price of that uniformity is preemption of stricter state rules, a feasibility review that can soften or delay the main standard, grandfathering that stretches out compliance, and the elimination of the Clean Water Act's permitting and enforcement backstop. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the state-preemption section, not the treatment standards, was the bill's defining feature.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Begich, a Democrat from Alaska, introduced the bill on June 21, 2012, joined on introduction by nine other senators from both parties, including Republicans Ayotte, Boozman, Snowe, Vitter, and Wicker and Democrats Inouye, McCaskill, and Rockefeller [S3].
The bill finished with 12 cosponsors, 8 Republicans and 4 Democrats [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction; the action history records no hearing, markup, or floor action afterward [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill received no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing regulatory framework stayed in place: states kept their authority over vessel discharges and the shipping industry did not get the single preemptive national standard it sought. The practical beneficiaries of the bill's death were the states with stricter ballast water rules and the people whose waters they protect.

for.name: Commercial shipping and maritime interests
for.role: Vessel operators seeking a single national discharge standard
for.what_they_did: Long sought to move vessel discharge regulation from Clean Water Act permitting to uniform Coast Guard standards and to preempt stricter state rules

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 21, 2012 and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the sponsor was a Democrat and the 12 cosponsors split 8 Republicans and 4 Democrats [S4]; the bill died of inaction, not opposition.

industries.note: The bill swaps Clean Water Act permits and any state-by-state rules for one set of Coast Guard standards, grandfathers installed treatment systems for their service life, and exempts many fishing, recreational, and small vessels. What the industry gains in uniformity and lower regulatory friction comes at the cost of stronger, state-set water protection for the public [S3].

Certification makes Coast Guard-approved systems the only legal compliance route, guaranteeing manufacturers a market as owners must buy certified technology to meet the ballast water standard. The requirement also serves the public purpose of treating ballast water to keep invasive species out [S3].

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and recreational vessel owners
industries.note: The bill exempts vessels under 79 feet, fishing vessels, and recreational boats from any permit or discharge standard, sparing them compliance costs without a direct cost to the public [S3].
